text: Data gravity pulls workloads toward wherever data already lives, so replication across clouds is the exception, not the default -- done for specific reasons, with real cost and complexity attached. This lesson covers why organizations take that on anyway, how the replication actually happens mechanically, and the consistency tradeoffs that come with moving data across real network distance.

Four real reasons show up again and again. Disaster recovery -- a second, independent copy in a different cloud survives a failure that a single-cloud copy can't. Low-latency reads -- users in Europe reading a replica in a European region perform far better than reading across an ocean. Compliance and sovereignty, which the next lesson covers in depth. And deliberate multi-cloud redundancy, so a business isn't fully dependent on one vendor's continued pricing and existence.

Three mechanisms cover almost every real cross-cloud replication setup. Native database replication, like Postgres logical replication, streams changes from a primary to a replica anywhere network connectivity reaches. Change data capture tools -- Debezium, AWS Database Migration Service, Azure Data Factory's change-tracking pipelines -- read the transaction log, not the live tables, and stream every insert, update, and delete as an event. And some managed databases build global replication directly in, like Cosmos DB multi-region writes and DynamoDB Global Tables. What to avoid is dual-writing from application code to two databases in two clouds -- a partial failure leaves the copies silently inconsistent with no systematic way to catch it.

Across real network distance between clouds, enforcing strict consistency -- where every write is instantly visible everywhere -- would mean every write waits on a distant replica's acknowledgment. That's prohibitively expensive, so essentially every cross-cloud system instead accepts eventual consistency: a write is immediately correct where it happened, and replicas converge shortly after. The harder question is multi-writer conflicts -- when the same record is updated in two places near-simultaneously. Last-writer-wins is the default in both Cosmos DB and DynamoDB Global Tables, keeping the later timestamp and discarding the other. Application-level merge logic and CRDTs handle it more carefully for data where losing an update silently isn't acceptable.

The simplest, most reliable answer is often architectural: give each record exactly one authoritative writer location, and only take on true multi-writer complexity when the business genuinely needs low-latency local writes everywhere at once. Next lesson turns to a case where replication location isn't a choice at all -- where the law decides where certain data has to physically live.
